items.content:
@cormacb 🆕 Why Large? Tiny LMs & Agents on Edge/Robotics — Cormac Brick, Google

https://t.co/HUkLpHUlaJ

The constraint on edge AI is not compute, it is RAM, and it is getting worse: phone makers are shipping less of it this year, and a 6GB Raspberry Pi costs 2.5 times what it did at launch. So Cormac Brick's team at Google AI Edge spends its effort making models small enough to fit. A 2 billion parameter Gemma, quantized to 2.9 bits per weight, runs on a Raspberry Pi at about 8 tokens per second and on a Qualcomm NPU fast enough for a few frames of vision a second.  

Below that sit tiny models, from 500 million parameters down to 50, that reach the older laptops and cheap devices where even a small model will not fit. They usually need fine tuning rather than prompting, but the payoff is real: a fine tuned Gemma turns free text into the right function call across ten actions at over 86% reliability, and putting a speech model in front gives you voice to function calling. One shipped example is an offline voice dictation app with no subscription, built on two sub billion Gemma models that also strip your ums and ahs.

items.content:
The Opus 5 system card itself is a fun PDF to parse. It's 193 pages and stacked with labeled and unlabeled charts 📊

LlamaParse does a surprisingly good job on agentic (1.25c per page) and agentic plus modes (5.6c per page). Take a look at some of the screenshots below. It can parse a variety of unlabeled line and bar charts with almost 100% accuracy. There are minor deltas with one or two datapoints, but the rest is pretty accurate machine-readable context that you can feed to downstream systems.

In contrast I also tried using Opus 5 itself to parse its own PDF. The chart accuracy is worse (20-30% reduction in ParseBench), and is a lot more expensive: it can cost anywhere from 8c to 33c+ per page depending on the thinking mode. 

If you're interested in giving LlamaParse a try, come check it out! https://t.co/XYZmx5TFz8

LlamaParse does a surprisingly good job on agentic (1.25c per page) and agentic plus modes (5.6c per page). Take a look at some of the screenshots below. It can parse a variety of unlabeled line and bar charts with almost 100% accuracy. There are minor deltas with one or two datapoints, but the rest is pretty accurate machine-readable context that you can feed to downstream systems.

In contrast I also tried using Opus 5 itself to parse its own PDF. The chart accuracy is worse (20-30% reduction in ParseBench), and is a lot more expensive: it can cost anywhere from 8c to 33c+ per page depending on the thinking mode.

Engine: Three.js r180 (v0.180.0) on WebGL2 — no game engine, no physi...
items.content:
@maximillian_dev From Claude:

Engine: Three.js r180 (v0.180.0) on WebGL2 — no game engine, no physics library. three is the only runtime dependency; the build tooling around it is Vite 7 for bundling, plus Playwright for the headless screenshot/profiling harness.

Almost everything you'd normally get from an engine was written by hand on top of Three's renderer:

- Rendering — Three's WebGLRenderer is used, but the pipeline on top is custom: HDR float targets, cascaded shadow maps packed into a sampler2DArray, an MRT depth/normal/velocity prepass, GTAO, TAA with YCoCg variance clipping, tile-dilated motion blur, a Karis bloom pyramid, GPU EV100 metering, and a procedural 33³ grade LUT into an AgX composite. Three's examples/jsm/postprocessing stack was deliberately not used.
- Physics — written from scratch, no Rapier/Ammo/Cannon: a binned-SAH BVH over the level's triangle soup, a swept-capsule character controller, an impulse-based rigid-body solver with CCD, and PBD ragdolls with distance/cone/twist constraints.
- Animation — procedural rather than Three's clip system: spring-driven weapon lag, recoil curves, reload sequences, foot IK, aim IK.

Sound: yes, entirely from scratch — synthesized live with the Web Audio API. There are zero audio files; the whole game deploys as index.html plus one JavaScript bundle, so there's nothing to load.

The audio subsystem builds its own synthesis toolkit — noise generators (white/pink/brown), oscillators, ADSR envelopes, biquad filter chains, waveshaper distortion, and convolution reverb driven by procedurally generated impulse responses. Gunshots are layered the way a real game sound is: a transient click, a low-frequency body thump, a bright crack, a noise-burst tail, and a separate mechanical bolt layer, with round-robin variation and pitch jitter off the seeded RNG so automatic fire never sounds like a looping sample. Beyond that it does distance modelling (near shots are all crack, distant ones lose highs and gain a rolling boom, with propagation delay), HRTF spatialisation via PannerNode, occlusion by raycasting from listener to source through the physics BVH and applying a lowpass, and a reverb send whose IR is chosen by probing the space.

items.content_html:
@AbdMuizAdeyemo The robotics industry calls it egocentric data. In other words, it is data of you doing something to manipulate the real world, like making a sandwich for lunch.

If they collect that data, then their world model knows how to make a sandwich for lunch. The more data you give it, the more things it's going to know.

And yeah, it can RAG and look at YouTube, but that data is not really egocentric most of the time.

items.content:
Satellite IoT brings visibility where terrestrial networks cannot reach.

If remote assets stay invisible, resilience is only a slogan, because teams cannot monitor what is moving or failing far from the networks they normally trust.

Microblog by @antgrasso about #SatelliteIoT 

The point is not to connect everything by satellite.

The point is to close the blind spots that make remote operations fragile.

When assets move across long routes or isolated regions, visibility is what turns distance into something manageable.

A sensor that reports location or equipment condition from a remote site gives teams time to act before a problem grows.

In logistics, this can mean adjusting a route earlier. In agriculture, it can mean seeing soil or weather conditions where normal connectivity is weak.

The same logic applies to energy systems.

Pipelines, grids, or offshore platforms need continuity even when terrestrial coverage is limited, because a hidden fault can quickly become an operational disruption.

Satellite IoT is valuable when visibility reaches the places where risk starts.

For remote operations, that is where resilience begins to move from intention to practice.

This textbook is organized around its 2 main themes:
[Amazon Summary]

1. Linear algebra and its applications: The chapters focus on the basics of linear algebra together with their common applications to singular value decomposition, matrix factorization, similarity matrices (kernel methods), and graph analysis. Numerous machine learning applications have been used as examples, such as spectral clustering, kernel-based classification, and outlier detection. The tight integration of linear algebra methods with examples from machine learning differentiates this book from generic volumes on linear algebra. The focus is clearly on the most relevant aspects of linear algebra for machine learning and to teach readers how to apply these concepts.

2. Optimization and its applications: Much of machine learning is posed as an optimization problem in which we try to maximize the accuracy of regression and classification models. The “parent problem” of optimization-centric machine learning is least-squares regression. Interestingly, this problem arises in both linear algebra and optimization, and is one of the key connecting problems of the two fields. Least-squares regression is also the starting point for support vector machines, logistic regression, and recommender systems. Furthermore, the methods for dimensionality reduction and matrix factorization also require the development of optimization methods. A general view of optimization in computational graphs is discussed together with its applications to back propagation in neural networks.

items.content:
- annoying beeps/rings/sounds constantly for every thing like passenger calls flight attendant button *ding* and everyone has to here it for some reason or when *ding* turbulence put your seatbelt on

- let passengers only select/order food and drinks from their seat with their phone, that saves a lot of time having flight attendants not have to take orders
- relatedly I'd strip out the entire entertainment system and just give people incredibly fast WiFi on their devices with Starlink, they can use their own apps to watch stuff on their phones or iPad

items.content:
It's very hard to escape this body when you live in the US unless you are willing to:

1) Pay more money for your food
2) Lift and move more (a lot more!)

I believe the US has some of the best food in the world, but you have to pay for the privilege.

I spend two to three months every year in Europe, and I can find good food at any price point. Sometimes, I eat without my normal restrictions, and my weight stays the same or increases very little.

I go back to the US and feel bloated after one week. It's ridiculous. 

There's something in our food. I don't know what it is, but you can't convince me there isn't.

Now, there's a price threshold beyond which you get amazing food in the States. This applies to both grocery stores and restaurants.

For example, in South Florida, it's really hard to find good food—great ingredients, proper cooking techniques, presentation, etc.—for less than $100 per person. There are exceptions, but most chain restaurants, where most people eat regularly, sell you garbage food that makes you fat and sick.

Grocery stores are the same. I visit one specific store where they regularly give you 10lbs of chicken drums for free when you spend $10 or more. Just think about the economics of this! I'm convinced that chicken was grown in a lab.

Another interesting thing I've noticed: If you go to a good restaurant ($100+ per person), you rarely see people who are out of shape.

So, it's a chore for Americans to stay fit. Much harder than in Europe, based on my experience. It's doable, but not cheap.
